# An actual sector cut-and-fill step with a strictly worsening section weight

This is a local ordinary planar deformation lemma. It preserves all
three cap-volume upper constraints and the joint ordinary profile while
strictly decreasing one normalized inverse-section weight. Its geometric
hypotheses are explicit. It is not a triangle reduction, does not assert
termination of repeated steps, and does not assert compatibility with
external mixed-integer fibers.

## 1. The permitted local geometry

Use normals v_1=(1,0), v_2=(0,1), v_3=(-1,-1), and let K be a convex
polygon with 0 in int K. Put

    q_i=|K intersect {v_i.x>=0}|,
    sigma_i=H_1(K intersect {v_i.x=0})/||v_i||,
    lambda_i=(1/sigma_i)/sum_j(1/sigma_j).

Let P=(0,h), h>0, be the upper endpoint of the vertical section.
Assume either that P lies in the relative interior of one polygon edge
R S, or that P is a polygon vertex with adjacent vertices R,S in the
counterclockwise order R,P,S. Require

    R=(r_x,r_y): r_x>0, r_y>0,
    S=(s_x,s_y): s_x<0, s_y>0, s_x+s_y>0.                         (1)

Thus R belongs to the double-capture sector {1,2}, and S belongs to
the adjacent single-capture sector {2}. These are ADJACENT open sectors
separated by the positive vertical cut ray. An edge whose endpoints
span additional cut rays does not satisfy the hypothesis.

For every sufficiently small epsilon>0 there is a convex polygon
K_epsilon with 0 in its interior such that

    |K_epsilon|=|K|,
    q_1(K_epsilon)=q_1(K)+s_x epsilon/2<q_1(K),
    q_2(K_epsilon)=q_2(K), q_3(K_epsilon)=q_3(K),                  (2)
    sigma_1(K_epsilon)=sigma_1(K)+epsilon,
    sigma_2(K_epsilon)=sigma_2(K),
    sigma_3(K_epsilon)=sigma_3(K).                                (3)

Consequently lambda_1(K_epsilon)<lambda_1(K). If lambda_1 was the
smallest normalized inverse weight, it remains the smallest and its
minimum strictly decreases.

## 2. Proof by one actual fill and one actual shave

Insert P_epsilon=(0,h+epsilon), or replace the vertex P by this point.
Call the resulting convex hull K_epsilon^+. For sufficiently small
epsilon the only new boundary pieces are R P_epsilon and P_epsilon S.
For an edge-interior P, this follows because the other polygon vertices
lie strictly on the inner side of that edge and all adjacent vertex
angles are strict. For an existing vertex P, all the strict adjacent
cross-product inequalities persist by continuity. In either case 0
stays strictly on the inner side of each new edge. Thus these statements
follow from finitely many strict inequalities, not an assumption about
an infinitesimal unconstrained boundary motion.

The old K lies in K_epsilon^+. In the edge-interior case this is immediate
from taking its convex hull with P_epsilon. In the vertex case the new
polygon still contains 0, and P is on [0,P_epsilon], so it contains
every old vertex. The added region is exactly the two triangles

    conv(R,P,P_epsilon), conv(S,P,P_epsilon),

up to shared edges. They lie on opposite sides of x=0. Their areas are

    d_12=r_x epsilon/2,
    d_2=-s_x epsilon/2,
    D=d_12+d_2=(r_x-s_x)epsilon/2.                               (4)

Their interiors lie in the two open sectors in (1), respectively,
because those sectors are convex and their non-ray vertices are strict.
They therefore have exactly the capture signatures {1,2} and {2}.
The fill increases (q_1,q_2,q_3) by (d_12,D,0).

The polygon vertex R remains a strict vertex for sufficiently small
epsilon. Choose an exposing linear functional for R strictly inside
its original normal cone. It continues to expose R uniquely after
the small fill. A sufficiently shallow parallel cut removes a cap
contained in the open quadrant {x>0,y>0}; the cut and its removed
region are disjoint from all three source lines. Such caps have positive
area and their area varies continuously and strictly with cut depth near
zero. Since D tends to zero, one may shave an actual such cap of EXACT
area D from K_epsilon^+. Denote the retained intersection by K_epsilon.

This shave has capture signature {1,2}. It removes D from q_1 and q_2,
and none from q_3. Together with (4) this proves (2). The shaved cap is
disjoint from the three source lines, so it changes none of their
sections. The fill touches neither y=0 nor x+y=0. Its only change on
x=0 is to extend the upper endpoint from P to P_epsilon; its opposite
endpoint is unchanged. This proves (3), including the normalized
diagonal section convention.

Finally lambda_1=x/(x+C), where x=1/sigma_1 and the positive number
C=1/sigma_2+1/sigma_3 is fixed. It strictly decreases when sigma_1
increases. The other two normalized weights increase, proving the
assertion about an initially minimal weight.

## 3. Exact preservation of the candidate constraints

Let k=|K|. Any collection q_i<=c k remains true by (2). If the sorted
masses are x<=y<=z, put F_K=x+y+z/4. This function is coordinatewise
nondecreasing in the unsorted masses: every order statistic is
coordinatewise nondecreasing, and all three coefficients are positive.
Therefore F_(K_epsilon)<=F_K. In particular F_K<=k is preserved exactly.
No appeal to a zero dual cost or a freely selected sector-area change
is involved; Section 2 constructs the actual convex body.

The same statement holds after interchanging the first two normals or
cyclically relabeling the three normals by the corresponding linear
coordinate change. Normalized section densities then acquire a common
area-Jacobian factor: they are derivatives of cap area with respect to
the same scalar threshold. Thus normalized inverse weights are
unchanged by that common factor.

## 4. A rational example inside both cap and profile constraints

Consider the counterclockwise quadrilateral

    P0=(-26/25,-49/50), P1=(49/25,-49/50),
    R=(1/2,1/2), S=(-26/25,101/50).

It is strictly convex and contains 0 in its interior. Its area is
453/100. Exact clipping gives

    q_1=374177/192500,
    q_2=763573/370000,
    q_3=10201/5000,

    sigma_1=3799/1925,
    sigma_2=7523/3700,
    sigma_3=101/50.

All q_i/k are strictly below 128/279. Also q_1<q_3<q_2 and

    k-F_K=3429703/113960000>0.

Here sigma_2 is largest, so lambda_2 is the smallest inverse weight.
Apply the lemma with x and y interchanged. The positive horizontal
section endpoint on P1 R is P=(147/148,0). Set

    epsilon=25/732008, tau=1/20,
    P_epsilon=P+(epsilon,0),
    R_1=(1-tau)R+tau P_epsilon,
    R_2=(1-tau)R+tau S.

The resulting actual polygon is

    conv(P0,P1,P_epsilon,R_1,R_2,S).

To check the exact equal-area shave, the fill area is
(37/50)epsilon=1/39568. The triangle at the old vertex R with
neighbors P_epsilon,S has area

    3/296-(19/25)epsilon.

The removed corner at edge fractions tau,tau has tau^2 times that
area, which equals 1/39568 for the chosen epsilon. All three vertices
of the removed triangle lie strictly in {x>0,y>0}.

Consequently the new polygon has the same area and satisfies exactly

    q_1^new=q_1, q_3^new=q_3,
    q_2^new=q_2-49/2928032,
    sigma_2^new=sigma_2+25/732008,
    sigma_1^new=sigma_1, sigma_3^new=sigma_3.

Its smallest normalized inverse weight therefore strictly decreases,
while all cap bounds and the joint profile stay feasible. This example
is not a violation of the desired 2/9 weight bound; it certifies that
the local feasible direction is a real convex-body operation inside
the proposed constraint set.

## 5. What this step does not establish

At a local minimum of a specified normalized inverse weight among
polygons under the displayed area and cap/profile constraints, the
corresponding cut endpoint cannot have the adjacent-sector geometry
(1). This is a proved local structural restriction.

It does not imply that all other boundary pieces can be eliminated.
For example, an edge joining two single-capture vertices may cross
multiple cut rays, so its outward motion changes several section chords
and is outside the lemma. Repeating the construction may introduce new
vertices. No bound on the number of steps, no global optimizer, and
no final triangle has been proved here.

## 6. Every strictly convex planar body admits the same actual step

Here K may be any strictly convex planar convex body with 0 in int K;
strict convexity means its boundary contains no nontrivial segment.
For each specified index i, there is an actual nearby convex body with
the same area, the other two cap masses and section densities unchanged,
its i-th cap mass strictly decreased, and its i-th section density
strictly increased. It therefore strictly decreases lambda_i while
preserving all the cap/profile inequalities in Section 3.

It suffices to use i=1 and the positive vertical endpoint P=(0,h).
Set P_epsilon=(0,h+epsilon) and L_epsilon=conv(K union {P_epsilon}).
We first prove the required locality rather than presuming it for a
body with possible flat faces:

    for every open neighborhood O of P,
    L_epsilon\K subset O for all sufficiently small epsilon>0.    (5)

Otherwise choose epsilon_j tending to zero and x_j in
(L_epsilon_j\K)\O. Compactness gives a subsequence with x_j tending
to x. For each j a separating unit functional n_j has
n_j.x_j>h_K(n_j). Pass to a subsequence with n_j tending to n. Since
x_j is in the convex hull, this strict inequality forces
n_j.P_epsilon_j>h_K(n_j). Passing to the limit gives n.P=h_K(n),
because P belongs to K. Also L_epsilon_j subset K+epsilon_j B_2,
so x belongs to K, and the limiting separating inequalities give
n.x=h_K(n). Thus P and x lie in the same support face of K. Strict
convexity makes that face the singleton {P}, contradicting x outside
the neighborhood O. This proves (5).

Choose O small enough that every point in it has y>0 and x+y>0.
The added region then has only the signatures {1,2} and {2} on its
right and left portions. Both portions have positive area. Indeed
P_epsilon lies outside K, and its exterior neighborhood intersects
the cone conv(P_epsilon,B(0,rho)) on both sides of x=0, where a fixed
small ball B(0,rho) is contained in K. Those two intersections have
positive area and lie in the added region. Denote their areas by
D_12 and D_2, and put D=D_12+D_2>0. Furthermore D tends to zero,
since L_epsilon subset K+epsilon B_2 and the outer parallel sets
decrease to K. Their volume convergence follows, for example, by
continuity from above of finite Lebesgue measure.

Choose a fixed boundary point R in the open quadrant {x>0,y>0},
for instance the boundary point on the positive diagonal ray. A
supporting functional ell at R exposes only R by strict convexity.
In particular ell.P<ell.R. Sufficiently shallow ell-caps of K are
contained in this open quadrant: otherwise a sequence of their
points tending away from R would give another point in that support
face by compactness. Fix one positive-depth such cap whose closed
neighborhood is disjoint from P. For sufficiently small epsilon,
(5) makes the added region disjoint from this fixed cap. Thus the
same cap on L_epsilon equals the original cap on K.

Its smaller parallel cap areas vary continuously from zero through a
fixed positive amount. Since D tends to zero, shave one of exact area
D. This is an actual halfspace intersection, is disjoint from all
three source lines, and has signature {1,2}. The final body's changes
are therefore

    Delta area=0,
    Delta(q_1,q_2,q_3)=(-D_2,0,0),
    Delta(sigma_1,sigma_2,sigma_3)=(epsilon,0,0).                  (6)

The section assertion follows as before: a point of L_epsilon on x=0
is a convex combination of P_epsilon with a point of K on x=0, so
the new upper endpoint is exactly P_epsilon. The other two section
lines do not meet the added or removed regions. The origin remains
interior because both alterations occur away from its fixed interior
ball. This proves the claimed general-body step.

In particular a strictly convex K cannot be a local minimum of any
specified lambda_i in the full class of convex bodies subject to
these inequalities. If i is an index of its smallest lambda, the
minimum over the three weights strictly decreases as well. The new
body need not be strictly convex; no minimum within the narrower
strictly convex class is being discussed.

This argument explicitly identifies why strict convexity matters:
with a nontrivial supporting face through P, the limiting x in the
proof of (5) need not equal P. The newly added region can then run
along that whole face and cross additional cut rays. The general
polygon or arbitrary-body triangle reduction remains unproved.
